To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the exposure of electrosprayed proteins in acidic or basic vapors can lead to significant changes of their charge state distributions.

the exposure of electrosprayed droplets to acidic vapors leads to the refolding of denatured proteins and that the exposure of basic vapors to acidic electrospray solutions results in the unfolding of native proteins.

the exposure of electrosprayed protein droplets in a counter-current drying gas to acidic or basic vapors, respectively leads to a rapid change in the observed charge states of proteins from high to low charge states that is consistent with the folding of initially denatured proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of protein conformational changes on the sub-millisecond time scale.
the study of the structure and function of proteins by means of electrospray ionization mass spectrometry and tandem mass spectrometry (ESI-MS and ESI-MS/MS).
the development of new methods for protein characterization and the application of these methods to problems in protein structure, folding, and function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed changes in charge state distribution are a function of a combination of the magnitude of pH change and the rates at which proteins can respond to the change.
the vapor treatment of electrospray proteins is a powerful tool for studying the folding kinetics of proteins.

the observed changes in the electrospray mass spectra of the proteins are a function of both the pH change induced by the vapor exposure and the rate of the protein's response to this change, which is dependent upon the magnitude of the initial solution pH change.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the exposure of initially denatured proteins to a basic or acidic vapor can lead to the refolding of the proteins in the gas-phase.

the exposure of electrosprayed protein droplets to vapors of basic or acidic reagents leads to changes in the observed protein charge states that are consistent with the folding of initially denatured proteins on a sub-millisecond time-scale.

the exposure to acidic vapors of electrospray solutions that have been acidified with trifluoroacetic acid leads to a decrease in the charge state distribution, and the exposure of electrosprayed solutions that have been basified with ammonium hydroxide to acidic vapors leads to an increase in the charge state distributions of the proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
electrospray droplet evaporation in the presence of a counter-current vapor can be used to access transient states in protein folding.

we have shown that electrospray droplet evaporation in the presence of acidic or basic vapors can be used to induce protein folding on the millisecond time scale, which is much faster than what can be accomplished in solution.

the exposure of electrosprayed droplets to basic or acidic vapor leads to significant changes in charge state distribution that can be used as a probe of the conformational state of the proteins in the electrospray droplet.
